hello.note: Reply: sijambo. Greet elders with shikamoo (they answer marahaba). Tourists mostly hear jambo.

please.note: When asking for something, naomba … (I request …) often sounds more natural.

thank_you.note: Asante sana: thank you very much. To several people: asanteni.

youre_welcome.note: The same word also means 'welcome' and 'come in'.

sorry.note: Pole shows sympathy (someone is hurt or tired); it is not an apology. For a real wrong: nisamehe.

excuse_me.note: Same word as for 'sorry': samahani covers both.

good_morning.note: Reply: nzuri. Also common: umeamkaje? (how did you wake up?)

how_are_you.note: Reply: nzuri (good). Casual among young people: mambo? — answer poa.

im_fine.note: The usual answer to habari? To hujambo? answer sijambo. Ask back: na wewe?

whats_your_name.note: Also common: unaitwa nani? (what are you called?)

nice_to_meet_you.note: Also: nimefurahi kukutana nawe (I'm glad to have met you).

where_from.note: Can also mean 'where are you coming from now?'. Clearer for a country: unatoka nchi gani?

im_from.note: In speech often natoka … For nationality: mimi ni Mkenya (I'm Kenyan).

speak_english.note: In Kenya also: unaongea Kiingereza? Written questions often start with je.

dont_understand.note: Also very common: sijaelewa (I haven't understood).

speak_slowly.note: Add zaidi for 'even more slowly': polepole zaidi.

where.note: Usually comes after the verb: unaenda wapi? (where are you going?)

what.note: Usually comes after the verb: unataka nini? (what do you want?)

when.note: Usually comes at the end: utarudi lini? (when will you come back?)

who.note: Also used to ask a name: jina lako ni nani?

how_much.note: Also common: ni shilingi ngapi? (how many shillings?)

can_you_help.note: Also polite and very common: naomba msaada (I'd like some help).

what_time.note: Swahili time counts from dawn: 7 am is saa moja (hour one), 8 am is saa mbili.

what_means.note: About a word: neno hili lina maana gani?

one.note: Changes with some nouns: mtu mmoja (one person), kitu kimoja (one thing).

four.note: Say both n's: n-ne. With people: watu wanne.

six.note: From Arabic, like saba and tisa, so it never changes: watu sita.

water.note: Drinking water: maji ya kunywa. Bottled water: maji ya chupa.

tea.note: Usually served sweet with milk. Black tea: chai ya rangi or chai kavu; in Kenya often strungi.

im_hungry.note: Literally 'I have hunger'; thirst works the same way: nina kiu.

menu_please.note: Naomba (I request) is the polite way to ask for anything; tafadhali is optional.

delicious.note: Agrees with the noun: chakula ni kitamu (food), chai ni tamu (tea). Sana means 'very'.

no_meat.note: Sili comes from kula (to eat). Same pattern: sili samaki (I don't eat fish).

enjoy_meal.note: The host's invitation to eat; people eating also say it to anyone passing by.

right.note: Kulia also means 'to cry'; context makes it clear.

stop_here.note: Literally 'drop me here'. Also: simama hapa (stop here).

hotel.note: In East Africa hoteli often means a simple eatery too. A guesthouse: nyumba ya wageni.

train_station.note: Also common: stesheni. Kituo alone is any stop or station, e.g. kituo cha basi (bus stop).

want_to_go.note: Softer: ningependa kwenda … (I'd like to go to …).

is_it_far.note: Answers: si mbali (it's not far), ni karibu (it's near).

one_ticket.note: On minibuses (matatu, daladala) you usually just pay the conductor (kondakta).

too_expensive.note: To bargain: punguza bei kidogo (lower the price a little).

cheaper.text: Una kitu cha bei nafuu zaidi?
cheaper.note: Rahisi (cheap, easy) also works: cha bei rahisi zaidi?

id_like_this.note: Hiki means 'this thing'. In a shop people also say nitachukua hiki (I'll take this).

pay_card.note: Mobile money (e.g. M-Pesa) is often more widely accepted than cards.

cash.note: Pesa alone means money. To pay cash: kulipa kwa pesa taslimu.

open.note: Signs may also read tuko wazi (we're open).

big.note: Agrees with the noun: nyumba kubwa (house), kitu kikubwa (thing), mtu mkubwa (person).

small.note: Agrees with the noun: nyumba ndogo, kitu kidogo, mtu mdogo. Kidogo also means 'a little'.

tomorrow.note: The day after tomorrow: kesho kutwa.

now.note: Right now: sasa hivi, though in practice it often means 'soon'.

good_evening.note: Reply: nzuri. Jioni runs from late afternoon to dusk.

good_night.note: Before sleep, also: lala salama (sleep well).

see_you_later.note: Often just tutaonana (we'll see each other).

every_day.note: Kila (every) comes before the noun: kila mtu (everyone).

call_police.note: Or: piga simu polisi! (phone the police).

need_doctor.note: Take me to hospital: nipeleke hospitali.

im_lost.note: Uses the -me- (perfect) tense: literally 'I have got lost'.

dont_feel_well.note: Also: ninaumwa (I'm ill). A headache: kichwa kinauma.

pharmacy.note: Dawa means medicine. In Kenya pharmacies are also called chemists.

hospital.note: A small clinic: zahanati or kliniki.

lost_phone.note: Kupoteza is to lose something; kupotea is to be lost yourself (nimepotea).

allergic.note: Mzio is the standard word; in speech many use the loanword aleji: nina aleji ya karanga (peanuts).

no_problem.note: Hakuna matata exists but is less common in daily speech. Casual: sawa (OK).

i_like_it.note: Just tried or seen it? Nimeipenda (I've come to like it) is very common.

im_tired.note: The kind reply is pole! (a word of sympathy).

im_happy.note: Also: nimefurahi (I'm pleased), e.g. at good news.

welcome.note: To several guests: karibuni! The reply is asante.

my_family.note: Possessives follow the noun: mama yangu (my mother), rafiki yangu (my friend).

mother.note: Also a respectful way to address any older woman. Parents: wazazi.

father.note: Also a respectful way to address an older man.

brother.note: Usually an older brother; a younger sibling is mdogo wangu. Ndugu covers any sibling or relative.

sister.note: Usually an older sister; a younger sibling is mdogo wangu. Also a friendly way to address a young woman.

child.note: Plural: watoto. My child: mwanangu. Son: mtoto wa kiume; daughter: mtoto wa kike.

friend.note: Same word for a man or a woman. Plural: marafiki.

this_is_my_friend.note: Same for a male or female friend. Huyu means 'this person'.

are_you_married.note: Asking a woman: umeolewa? Kuoa is what a man does, kuolewa what a woman does.

have_children.note: Answers: nina watoto wawili (I have two children), sina watoto (I have none).

monday.note: Literally 'day three': the Swahili week counts from Saturday.

tuesday.note: Literally 'day four'. Say both n's: Juma-n-ne.

thursday.note: From Arabic, like Ijumaa, so it breaks the Juma- pattern.

friday.note: The Muslim day of prayer. Say every vowel: I-ju-ma-a.

saturday.note: Literally 'day one': the count of the week starts here.

weekend.note: In everyday speech, especially in Kenya, wikendi is very common.

what_day.note: Answer: leo ni Ijumaa. For the date: leo ni tarehe ngapi?

eleven.note: Literally 'ten and one'; up to 19 the pattern is the same: kumi na tisa.

twelve.note: With people: watu kumi na wawili.

twenty.note: From Arabic, like all the tens up to ninety. 21 is ishirini na moja.

thirty.note: The th is said as in English 'think'.

fifty.note: The noun comes first: shilingi hamsini (fifty shillings).

hundred.note: Often just mia. Mia mbili is 200, mia tano is 500.

thousand.note: Often just elfu. Prices are often in thousands: elfu kumi (10,000).

how_old.note: Also: una umri gani? (what is your age?)

years_old.note: Literally 'I have … years': nina miaka thelathini (I'm 30).

red.note: Agrees with the noun: shati jekundu (shirt), kitabu chekundu (book).

blue.note: Also spelled buluu. It never changes: shati la bluu. Sky blue: samawati.

green.note: From jani (leaf). It never changes: shati la kijani.

yellow.note: Also manjano (originally 'turmeric'). It never changes: shati la njano.

black.note: Agrees with the noun: shati jeusi (shirt), kitabu cheusi (book).

white.note: Agrees with the noun: shati jeupe (shirt), kitabu cheupe (book).

what_colour.note: Pointing at something: hii ni rangi gani? (what colour is this?)

this_one.note: Agrees with the item: hiki for kitu (thing), hii for nguo or chupa. Hii is widely understood.

that_one.note: For nguo or chupa: ile. Near the listener rather than far away: hicho or hiyo.

another_one.note: Nyingine fits soda, chai or a bottle; for kitu say kingine. Also: moja tena (one more).

its_hot.note: Joto is the heat of the weather; hot water is maji ya moto.

its_cold.note: I'm cold: nina baridi or nasikia baridi.

its_raining.note: Literally 'rain is falling'. Also short: kunanyesha.

weather_today.note: Hali ya hewa, literally 'state of the air', is the usual word for the weather.

beautiful_day.note: About the weather itself: hali ya hewa ni nzuri leo.

umbrella.note: Plural: miavuli. Used against the sun as much as the rain.

summer.note: East Africa has dry and rainy seasons; kiangazi is the hot dry one. Also: majira ya joto.

winter.note: East Africa has no real winter; on the coast the cool June–August season is kipupwe.

have_reservation.note: Literally 'I have reserved a room'. In everyday speech many just say nina booking.

room.note: Plural: vyumba. For one person: chumba cha mtu mmoja; for two: cha watu wawili.

passport.note: On official forms: hati ya kusafiria.

luggage.note: Singular: mzigo (one bag or load). A suitcase: sanduku.

wifi_password.note: In speech most people use the English word: password ya Wi-Fi ni ipi?

check_out_time.text: Muda wa kuondoka ni saa ngapi?
check_out_time.note: Mind Swahili time: saa tano asubuhi is 11 am. Hotels also just say check-out.

bus.note: Plural: mabasi. A minibus is a matatu (Kenya) or daladala (Tanzania).

next_train.note: Inayofuata: 'the one that follows'. For a bus: basi linalofuata ni saa ngapi?

is_this_seat_free.note: Literally 'does this seat have someone?'; hakina mtu means it's free. Also: kuna mtu hapa?

what_do_you_do.note: Also: kazi yako ni nini? (what is your job?)

i_work_in.note: Speech often uses kwenye: ninafanya kazi kwenye benki. A type of work: kazi ya mauzo (sales).

im_student.note: Same for men and women. A university student is also called mwanachuo.

office.note: At the office: ofisini, as in niko ofisini (I'm at the office).

meeting.note: A work meeting is often kikao: niko kikaoni (I'm in a meeting).

im_busy.note: Casual: niko bize. Also: nimebanwa (I'm tied up).

day_off.note: Longer leave or holiday: likizo. Casually: leo niko off (I'm off today).

colleague.note: Literally 'my fellow worker'; same for men and women. Often just mwenzangu.

good_job.note: Also very common: umefanya vizuri! (you did well). Casual: safi sana!

table_for_two.note: Also: tunaomba meza ya watu wawili (we'd like a table for two).

what_recommend.note: Also natural: chakula gani kizuri hapa? (which food is good here?)

not_spicy.note: Pilipili is chilli. Just a little: pilipili kidogo.

vegetarian_food.note: A vegetarian: mlaji mboga. Careful: mboga can mean any side dish, even a meat stew.

more_water.note: Or: niongezee maji (top up my water).

no_sugar.note: Tea often comes already sweetened, so ask early. A little sugar: sukari kidogo.

im_full.note: Add asante to be polite. Hosts may insist: ongeza! (have more!)

takeaway.note: Literally 'wrap it for me'. In Kenya also: nipakie, or ni ya kubeba (it's to carry).

it_was_delicious.note: Agrees with the noun: for tea, chai ilikuwa tamu. Add sana for 'very'.

keep_change.note: Chenji (from English) is the everyday word. Also: usinirudishie chenji (don't give me change).

head_hurts.note: Also common: kichwa kinauma, or naumwa kichwa.

have_fever.note: Homa can also mean a flu-like illness; homa ya malaria is malaria.

medicine.note: Same word for one or many. To take medicine: kunywa dawa or kumeza dawa (swallow).

call_ambulance.note: Formal word: gari la wagonjwa. Shouting to a crowd: iteni ambulensi!

dentist.note: Meno means teeth; one tooth is jino. Toothache: jino linauma.

need_rest.note: Also: nataka kupumzika kidogo (I want to rest a bit).

feel_better.note: Also very common: nimepata nafuu (I've got better). Nafuu also means 'cheap'.

get_well.note: The usual wish to a sick person, literally 'be ill gently'. Also: upone haraka!

lets_meet.note: Add a time or place: tukutane kesho (let's meet tomorrow).

are_you_free.note: Nafasi means room or time. Answers: nina nafasi (I'm free), sina nafasi (I'm not).

call_me.note: Casual: nipigie. Text me: nitumie ujumbe.

your_number.text: Namba yako ya simu ni ipi?
your_number.note: In Kenya also nambari. Very common: naomba namba yako (may I have your number?)

see_you_soon.note: Casual among friends: tuonane! or baadaye!

have_nice_day.note: Often just siku njema! To several people: muwe na siku njema!

happy_birthday.note: Also heard: siku njema ya kuzaliwa!

thanks_a_lot.note: To several people: asanteni sana. Warmer still: nashukuru sana (I'm very grateful).

miss_you.note: Literally 'I have remembered you'. Add sana for 'so much'. Casual: nimekumisi.
